question.leadin: Answer some questions about the newspaper Avanti!
question.text: Although he had formerly edited it, this fascist leader banned the publication of Avanti! when he took power. Nicknamed "Il Duce", he led the Blackshirts during the March on Rome.
question.clue: This former leader and his mistress Claretta Petacci were killed by partisans in the village of Giulino di Mezzegra near Lake Como.

swap.leadin: One noblewoman from this family was blamed for instigating a massacre of thousands of Huguenots in France on St. Bartholomew's Day.
swap.text: Name this European family to which Catherine, the wife of King Henry II, belonged. Cosimo established this family's dominance over the city of Florence during the Renaissance.
swap.answerHtml: Medici [MEH-dih-chee] family (accept Catherine de’ Medici or Cosimo de’ Medici )
swap.clue: People with this last name founded a Platonic Academy and were targeted in the Pazzi Conspiracy.

question.leadin: This bearded warrior led the Expedition of the Thousand while conquering the Kingdom of Two Sicilies for King Victor Emmanuel II.
question.text: Name this leader of the Red Shirts during Italian unification.
question.clue: This man allied with Brazil and the Colorados during the Uruguayan Civil War, thus earning the nickname "Hero of Two Worlds."

swap.text: Martin Waldseemuller named America after this man who explored the Brazilian territory.
swap.clue: In the Mundus Novus, this man informed Lorenzo de Medici that the land that he discovered was not Asia, but a new landmass.

question.text: This blind Doge took part in the Sack of Constantinople during the Fourth Crusade, but he and the forces of Baldwin I would later be defeated at the Battle of Adrianople.
question.clue: This leader refused rulership of the newly created Latin Empire, instead placing his fellow crusader Baldwin of Flanders on the throne.

swap.leadin: In this book, the author concludes that "men forget more easily the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony."
swap.text: Name this political treatise which also claims "it is far safer to be feared than loved." It is the most famous work of Niccolo Machiavelli.
swap.clue: Chapter eight praises the example of Agathocles, and another leader praised in this work is Cesare Borgia.

question.leadin: Answer the following about some prominent Italian political families of the Renaissance.
question.text: The Pazzi conspiracy attempted to overthrow this banking family by assassinating two of its members, Giuliano and Lorenzo the Magnificent. It first gained control over Florence under the leadership of Cosimo.
question.clue: A woman from this family is credited with instigating the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre, and popes from this family reigned during the rise of Martin Luther and Charles V's sack of Rome.

swap.leadin: An artistically inclined member of this family named Galeazzo Maria was murdered in 1476.
swap.text: Name this family whose most famous member was nicknamed "The Moor."
swap.clue: Prominent members included one who was briefly exiled after trying to displace Bona of Savoy; the cardinal Ascanio; and someone who married the daughter of the duke of Ferrara, Beatrice d'Este, in 1491.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the history of an island.
question.text: Its notable kings included William the Good and his successor, Tancred. In 1282 its people revolted against its French occupiers in what is known as its namesake Vespers.
question.clue: The Peace of Caltabellotta resulted in Charles the Lame renouncing the throne of this place, after which it was ruled as Trinacria by Frederick III.

swap.text: Engineered by Peter III of Aragon, it was ended by the Peace of Caltabellota, which put Frederick III on the throne. For 15 points, name this conflict, begun during the ringing of bells for a liturgical hour, in which Angevin rule of a Mediteranean island ended.
swap.clue: That king attempted to end this conflict by challenging Peter III of Aragon to personal combat with Edward I serving as the judge of the contest.

question.leadin: In A World Lit Only By Fire, historian William Manchester's off-the-cuff embellishments of this event include the fantastic claim that its participants received prizes in accordance with their respective levels of sexual prowess.
question.text: Name this hedonistic party held in the Apostolic Palace in 1501. This famed orgy was named for the objects that "fifty honest prostitutes" attempted to pick up off the floor while crawling between flaming candles.
question.answerHtml: the Banquet of the Chestnuts [both parts are necessary; or the Ballet of the Chestnuts]
question.clue: One of Cesare Borgia's most infamous acts was this debauched party. Cesare invited fifty prostitutes to this event, which was named for the items strewn on the ground for the courtesans to pick up.

swap.leadin: Rodrigo of this family served as Pope Alexander VI.
swap.text: What is this family of Spanish origin which included the Cardinal Cesare who convened the papal orgy known as the Banquet of Chestnuts?
swap.clue: One member of this family authored the Treaty of Tordesillas and had his rival Savonarolla executed.

question.text: Mutinous Habsburg soldiers sacked Rome during a conflict named for this organization. Pope Clement VII united France, England, Venice, Milan, and Florence into this 1526 alliance to expel Charles V from Italy.
question.clue: Much of Flemish autonomy was lost during the Peace of the Ladies, an agreement negotiated by Margaret of Austria and Louise of Savoy during a war named for this alliance. Francis I founded this alliance to counterbalance Hapsburg influence.

swap.leadin: In a letter to his father, this man explained that he entered a religious order because he "could not stand the great wickedness of the blind people of Italy."
swap.text: Name this Dominican friar whose followers, the Piagnoni, supported moralistic campaigns like the Bonfire of the Vanities. After a trial by fire was stopped by rain, this man lost popular support and was executed in 1498.
swap.clue: He increased his authority by predicting the invasion of Charles VIII, and the Arrabbiati formed in opposition to him.

question.leadin: This woman was the only daughter of Henry I, and her son was recognized as heir to the throne at the Treaty of Wallingford.
question.text: Name this woman who escaped from Oxford Castle across the frozen Thames during one engagement of a protracted civil war known as the Anarchy.
question.clue: This leader was put under siege in Oxford Castle, but escaped by crossing the Isis on foot.

swap.text: A condottiero named Francesco began this dynasty after Filippo Maria Visconti produced no heir. Leonardo da Vinci was employed by Ludovico, a member of this ruling dynasty of Milan.
swap.clue: One member of this family implemented the Wallach Reform while Queen of Poland.

question.leadin: Answer the following about Italy in the 1970s.
question.text: In the late 1970s, Enrico Berlinguer's ("bare-leen-GWER's") Italian Communist Party and Aldo Moro's Christian Democracy unexpectedly formed a coalitionary alliance known by this two-word term.
question.answerHtml: “historic compromise” [or “compromesso storico”; accept Third Phrase or Terza Fase; accept Democratic Alternative or Alternativa Democratica]
question.clue: This unexpected alliance between the PCI and Christian Democracy.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about food and cooking during the Italian Renaissance.
swap.text: This humanist scholar's diet book De vita uses the doctrine of signature to argue for eating foods based on their appearances, suggesting eating walnuts since they look like the brain. This scholar founded the Florentine Academy in an attempt to revive Platonic thought.

question.leadin: You, Ted Gioia, and a time machine. Join the thuggish Gioia clan and answer these questions about one of the two Sicilies.
question.text: This Norman kicked the Byzantines out of Italy in 1071 and died while on a bender in the Greek islands sieging Cephallonia.
question.clue: Soon after that, he reconciled with the Papacy and was invested as duke at the Council of Melfi.

swap.text: After Francesco Sforza, he concluded this treaty in 1454 between Milan and Venice, which established permanent boundaries amongst Italian states and lasted until the invasion of Charles VIII in 1494.
